summary: Canada's first lighthouse site: a French stone tower lit in 1734, lost in 1758, then a 1923 concrete tower, automated in 1990, on Lighthouse Point at Louisbourg.

lens.note: Historic lenses from the lighthouse (Rowlett); which lens is not stated.

structures.note: Mortared field stone; wooden lantern burned 1736; rebuilt 1738 with stone and brick lantern; damaged 1758 and never repaired. Foundations stabilised 1964 and 1985.
Second light on the same hill; Parks Canada dates it 1847-1923; burned June 1923.
Reinforced concrete; designed 1917; first lit 1 February 1924; O'Shea gives 14.5 m; Rowlett gives 17 m (55 ft).

staffing.note: Keepers until 1990, when fully automated (Parks Canada).

access.note: Site open, tower closed. Parking at the end of Havenside Road.

events.note: Construction of the stone tower began (Parks Canada); completed in 1734.
Lit 1 April 1734, reportedly seen for six leagues at sea (O'Shea); Parks Canada gives 16 km.
Fire around midnight 11-12 September destroyed the wooden lantern.
Fireproof stone and brick lantern completed July 1738 at a cost of 12,100 livres.
New England besiegers built a battery near the light; the tower was not damaged.
Heavily damaged in the British siege; repair recommended but never carried out.
The French light never operated again.
Second light built on the same hill after a petition by Thomas Jost and merchants near Sydney (Lighthouse Friends); Parks Canada dates it 1847.
First-order siren, operated by compressed air, put into operation 18 February 1902.
Fire on 3 June 1923 destroyed the 1842 wooden light (O'Shea; Marine report). Rowlett gives 1922.
Temporary light, 45 ft high, on the roof of the fog alarm building; occulting white every 12 seconds, visible 10 miles.
Concrete tower and keepers' double dwelling replace the burned light; New light operated 1 February 1924.
Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada plaque for the 18th-century light mounted on the concrete tower.
Keepers watched over the light until 1990, when it became fully automated.
Recognised as a Federal Heritage Building.
Extensive refurbishment of the 1923 tower began in November 2023.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The first light is dated 1734 by O'Shea, Parks Canada and the Lighthouse Friends history. Construction began in 1730 (Parks Canada) and the record's 1734 stands.
The CCG list gives LFl W 6s for the present tower; Rowlett gives a white flash every 10 seconds; the record's Wikidata entry gives Fl W 15s and OSM gives Fl W 10s. The story uses the CCG list.
The 1842 light burned on 3 June 1923 according to O'Shea and the 1924 Marine report. Rowlett gives 1922. The story uses 1923.
Lighthouse Friends and O'Shea give 1842 for the second light; Parks Canada gives 1847. The story says 1842 and notes Parks Canada's date.
O'Shea gives about 14.5 m for the 1923 tower; Rowlett gives 17 m (55 ft), matching the record. The story gives Rowlett's height in the structure data and notes O'Shea in the text.
Lighthouse Friends names Jean Grenard as the first keeper; O'Shea and Parks Canada say soldiers tended the fire first (1733). The story gives both.
Rowlett names the Canadian Coast Guard as owner and the Louisbourg Lighthouse Society as site manager. The record's agency is consistent with the CCG.

O'Shea says Little Brewster in Boston (1713) was the first on the coast of North America; Lighthouse Friends gives 1716 for Boston. The story does not use the claim except as the Parks Canada wording for Canada.

notes_for_editor: Checked 2026-10-27 against the cached Parks Canada Lighthouse Point page, the Lighthouse Friends page (ID=1406), O'Shea's French-period summary, O'Shea's Part I (1923-24 construction), the Lighthouse Directory Nova Scotia entry, the CCG List of Lights entry H3344 and the Marine reports (1903v37i8p21_0139 p. 75 scan 88; 1925v61i5p28_1773 p. 80 scan 87, 'Louisburg Lightstation'). Disagreements now stated in the text: second light 1842 (O'Shea, LF) vs 1847 (Parks Canada); fire 3 June 1923 (O'Shea Part I) vs 2 June (LF) and 1922 (Directory); first light in service 1 Feb 1924 (O'Shea Part I, Marine 1924 report) vs 20 Feb (LF); tower height: O'Shea 'almost 55 feet' with 14.5 m (the two do not convert), Directory 17 m (55 ft), List 15.4 m; Grenard's start 1733 (O'Shea) vs 1734 (LF); first keepers soldiers (Parks, O'Shea) vs Grenard as first keeper (LF). The sources give distances in leagues (O'Shea, and his own wording, 'six leagues' and 'four leagues'); they are kept as printed, not converted to nautical miles. Page check: the 1923-24 report page 'Louisburg Lightstation' is on scan 87 printed 80 with no '?'; the 1902-03 'Louisburg fog alarm' entry is on scan 88 printed 75 per the report's table of contents (the OCR head reads 75?). The 1902 siren is described in the Marine report as 'a first order siren', and the story says first-order; LF says first-class. The R. Forgeron, Covey and Tanner keeper roles are from O'Shea Part I and LF; no personal details are given. Forgeron (1966-1990) is a keeper whose service ended after 1960; he is named only in role. The 1923 light's Louisbourg 'E. M. Dickson' is the contractor (O'Shea, LF); the 1923 Marine reference to a Captain E. M. Dickson is not used. Wikipedia not cited. Six chapters, all with material.
